content: Passage 1 Coagulation necrosis is characterized by hypereosinophilia and nuclear changes such as pyknosis, followed by karyorrhexis and karyolysis. This process ultimately results in the total loss of nuclei and the disappearance of cytoplasmic cross-striations. These changes are typically first observed within 4 to 12 hours following myocardial infarction. Necrotic myocytes may retain their striations for an extended period. Neutrophilic infiltration, indicative of acute inflammation, along with edema and hemorrhage, also becomes apparent within the 4 to 12-hour window, though these changes are generally more prominent closer to 12 hours. The interstitial space at the margin of the infarcted area is initially infiltrated by neutrophils. Subsequently, lymphocytes and macrophages migrate to the site, where they phagocytose the necrotic myocyte debris. The necrotic region is progressively surrounded and invaded by granulation tissue, which eventually replaces the infarcted area with a fibrous or collagenous scar. This process is a hallmark of wound healing. The interstitial space, or the extracellular space outside of blood vessels, may also become infiltrated with red blood cells. By 3 to 10 days post-infarction, macrophages, lymphocytes, eosinophils, fibroblasts, and capillaries begin to infiltrate the periphery of the infarcted area. Contraction band necrosis, which is characterized by hypereosinophilic transverse bands of precipitated myofibrils in dead myocytes, is typically observed at the edges of an infarct or in cases of reperfusion, such as after thrombolytic therapy. Passage 2 Acute bronchitis can be caused by viral, bacterial, or environmental factors. Among these, viral infections are the most common cause, with the influenza virus being the leading overall etiological agent. Other causes of acute bronchitis are predominantly viral and include the following: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) Coronavirus Enterovirus
